rationale: Ethnographic qualitative study (participant-observation, semistructured interviews in 18 households, community meetings, and key-informant interviews with officials and growers) in Baja California's San Quintin Valley. Among legal and regulatory mechanisms affecting domestic water access, fees_tariffs_subsidies clearly dominates: the analysis contrasts state desalination, electricity, and well-meter subsidies for export agribusinesses under CNA with full cost-recovery policies enforced on colonia residents by the state urban utility CESPE (proposed 300% and enacted 115% flat-rate tariff increases, unsubsidized $227 household meter fees, three-part connection/piping/meter charges, and priced barrel quotas), alongside secondary discussions of decentralized agency mandates under the 1992 National Water Law (institutional_structure_coordination), weak CNA enforcement against unpermitted agricultural wells (enforcement_sanctions), and captured watershed councils/COTAS (participation_assistance). Outcomes are co-equally multi-dimensional (multiple), centered on effective_access (declining water quantity and quality from salinity and unfiltered muddy tap water, severe service intermittency, and barrel rationing) alongside economic_access (farmworker households spending ~14% of income on trucked water, tariff burden, and unaffordable meter charges) and primary_connection (40% of colonias lacking piped running water).
